passage: In the village high school, Shalini raised her hand in front of Kavitha ma'am and said she thought the group project should be done in pairs instead. Kavitha ma'am said, "We are doing it in fours. That is settled." Shalini felt a frown pulling at her brow and smoothed it with a quick breath, saying "Okay, ma'am." But her forehead stayed tense, and a line stayed between her eyes. After class Kavitha ma'am called her back. "Your face and your words were saying different things," she said. Shalini took a breath. "I think pairs would let everyone work, ma'am. In fours, one person does nothing." Kavitha ma'am nodded slowly, and said she would think about it.

passage:
At debate club, Nazia Ma'am read out the sides for Friday. "Deepika, you'll argue that homework should be banned."
Deepika's eyebrows pulled together. She hated that side; she thought homework helped. Then she remembered Ma'am's face last week when Rakesh had rolled his eyes, and she smoothed her forehead flat. She nodded.
But Nazia Ma'am had seen the little line between her brows, which hadn't quite gone away. "Deepika? You look like you've swallowed a lemon."
A few people laughed. Deepika took a breath. "Ma'am, honestly, I disagree with this side. I think homework helps. Can I say why, and then still argue it?"
Ma'am smiled. "That's better than a frown. Tell me."
Deepika explained. Ma'am listened, then said, "Good. Arguing the side you disagree with will make your real view sharper." Deepika nodded, this time meaning it.

qa.q: What side did Nazia Ma'am give Deepika?
qa.a: That homework should be banned.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she smoothed her forehead flat?
qa.a: She felt annoyed and in disagreement but also cautious, trying to avoid looking rude like Rakesh; the line between her brows showed the tension still there.

qa.q: Why did saying the disagreement out loud work better than the smoothed face?
qa.a: Words made the disagreement clear and polite, so Ma'am could respond with a reason, instead of guessing from a half-hidden frown.

qa.q: How might Nazia Ma'am see Deepika's spoken disagreement?
qa.a: Ma'am seemed to welcome it and respect Deepika more, seeing it as mature rather than rude.

grounding: A teenager tries to smooth a frown when disagreeing with a teacher, then learns naming the disagreement is clearer.

Dear Kishore Sir,
I'm writing because I didn't say this yesterday at the team meeting.
When you moved me from striker to defence, I kept my face blank. I thought if I frowned, you'd think I was being disrespectful. But I could feel my forehead going tight the whole time, and I think you noticed, because you asked if I was okay and I said "fine."
I'm not fine with it. I've scored four goals this season, and I don't understand the change. I'm not trying to argue. I just want to know why, and whether I can earn the striker spot back.
Could we talk before practice on Thursday?
Thanks,
Vijay

qa.a: Four goals.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling while keeping a blank face at the meeting?
qa.a: Vijay felt upset and confused about the position change, but hid the frown to avoid seeming disrespectful.

qa.q: Why is Vijay's email a better choice than the blank face?
qa.a: It puts the disagreement into clear, respectful words and asks for a reason, which a tight forehead alone could not do.

qa.q: How might Kishore Sir see the email?
qa.a: Kishore Sir will likely see it as mature and respectful, and may be glad to explain the decision now that the feeling behind the blank face is clear.

grounding: In an email, a teenager explains hiding a frown when disagreeing with a coach, and chooses to name the disagreement in words.

"Salma, you asked why Papa and I were quiet at dinner. Okay, here's what happened.
Papa said I have to join the extra maths tuition on Saturdays. I really didn't want to, because that's my only free day for art class. I tried to keep my face normal so it wouldn't turn into a fight. But he said, 'Gurpreet, your forehead is saying no even if your mouth is saying okay.'
I laughed, but then I just said it. 'Papa, I disagree. I think art helps me too, and I need one free day.'
He was quiet for a bit. Then he said, 'Maybe tuition on Sunday mornings, then.'
So that's why. I, Gurpreet, used words instead of my forehead, and it actually worked."

qa.a: Art class.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling while trying to keep a normal face?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt frustrated and worried about starting a fight, so tried to hide the disagreement.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do that helped the talk with Papa?
qa.a: Gurpreet stopped hiding the frown and calmly said the disagreement and the reason out loud.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Gurpreet explained?
qa.a: Papa probably felt surprised but respected, and he chose to find a middle path.

grounding: A teenager tells a cousin how Gurpreet tried to hide a frown from Papa, then named the disagreement in words.

passage: I'm Ganga, Sahil's cousin, and I was at their dinner table when Chacha said the Goa trip with Sahil's friends was off because exams were close. Sahil said, "Okay, Papa." He was smiling slightly, but I could see a small muscle jumping in his forehead, and his eyebrows kept pulling together and then smoothing out, as if he were ironing them flat. Chacha didn't notice; he was busy with the rasam. After dinner Sahil sat on the balcony for a long time. Then he went back in and said, "Papa, I said okay, but I don't agree. I've finished revising three subjects. Can we talk about it?" Chacha looked surprised, then pulled out a chair. I don't know how it ended, but they talked for an hour.

qa.a: Sahil was probably frustrated and disappointed about the cancelled trip, trying to hide it behind a slight smile and 'Okay, Papa'.

qa.a: Saying 'I don't agree' and giving his reason put the disagreement into words Chacha couldn't miss, which opened a real talk.

qa.q: How might Chacha have read Sahil's first "Okay, Papa"?
qa.a: Busy with the rasam, Chacha likely took it as easy agreement, missing the tense forehead Ganga saw.
